concepts.def: The low-level ionising radiation that is around us all of the time. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, and from man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.

Sources that are not the result of human activity, such as rocks and cosmic rays from space. Rocks in the ground and in building materials contain radioactive isotopes, so some radiation is always present.

Ionising radiation that arrives at the Earth from space. The atmosphere absorbs much of it, so the dose from cosmic rays is greater at high altitude than at sea level. Cosmic rays are a natural source of background radiation.
Sources that are present because of human activity, such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and from nuclear accidents. They add to the natural background rather than replacing it.

Radioactive material thrown into the atmosphere by nuclear weapons testing or by a nuclear accident, which then settles onto the ground and onto vegetation over a wide area. Fallout is a man-made source of background radiation.

concepts.term: Effect of occupation on radiation dose
concepts.def: Some jobs bring extra exposure to radiation, so the dose a person receives depends partly on their occupation. Radiographers, nuclear industry workers and aircrew, for example, receive higher annual doses than most other workers.

concepts.term: Effect of location on radiation dose
concepts.def: The level of background radiation varies from place to place, so dose depends partly on where a person lives or travels. Ground and buildings of granite release more radon gas, and exposure to cosmic rays rises with altitude.
A measure of the risk of harm to body tissue as a result of exposure to ionising radiation. It depends on both the amount of radiation absorbed and the type of radiation the body has been exposed to.
The unit in which radiation dose is measured. A dose stated in sieverts describes the risk to the body, not how radioactive a source is; the activity of a source is measured separately in becquerels.
A smaller unit of radiation dose, used because everyday doses are far below one sievert. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so a dose given in mSv is divided by 1000 to convert it into Sv.
Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values, from small fractions of a second for some isotopes to many thousands of millions of years for others.

The hazard from a radioactive material depends on its half-life. A short half-life means a high activity that falls away quickly, so the material is intensely radioactive at first but soon becomes much safer. A long half-life means a lower activity that persists, so the material stays hazardous for a very long time.
Nuclear radiations are used in medicine for the exploration of internal organs and for the control or destruction of unwanted tissue.

A substance containing a radioactive isotope that is taken into the body so that an internal organ can be explored. A gamma emitter with a short half-life is used, because gamma radiation passes out of the body to a detector and the activity soon falls away.

The use of nuclear radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue such as a tumour. A high dose of gamma radiation is directed at the tumour from outside the body, or an implanted source is placed so that the dose is concentrated where it is needed.

The risk people believe a nuclear radiation carries is often different from the risk shown by data. Evaluating a medical use means comparing the dose received, and its consequences, with the benefit of the diagnosis or treatment and with the risk of doing nothing.

mcqs.q: Which statement about background radiation is correct?
options: It is around us all of the time, from natural and from man-made sources.
It is present only in an area that a nuclear accident has affected.
It exists only because people have built reactors and weapons.
It is found only in places where uranium-bearing rock lies.
mcqs.explain: Background radiation is continuously present, and it has both natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space and man-made sources such as fallout.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?
options: Fallout still present from earlier nuclear weapons tests
Cosmic rays that reach the Earth's surface from space
Radioactive waste kept in a store at a power plant
Radiation produced by an X-ray machine in a hospital
mcqs.explain: Cosmic rays from space are named in the specification as a natural source of background radiation, alongside rocks.

mcqs.q: An accident at a nuclear power station releases radioactive material that settles over nearby farmland. How should this contribution to the background radiation there be classified?
options: As natural, because the isotopes also occur in rocks
As natural, since the fallout now lies in soil
As man-made, because human activity released it
As neither, because the material has spread widely
mcqs.explain: The specification lists the fallout from nuclear accidents as a man-made source; the classification depends on origin, not on where the material ends up.

mcqs.q: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?
options: Cosmic rays from space and rocks lying in the earth
Rocks in the ground and waste from nuclear accidents
Cosmic rays from space and fallout from weapons tests
Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents
mcqs.explain: These are exactly the two man-made sources named in the specification.

mcqs.q: A radiographer in a hospital records a higher annual radiation dose than an office worker who lives in the same street. What is the best explanation?
options: Everyone receives the same dose, so the readings must be faulty.
Her occupation exposes her to radiation that the office worker never meets.
Radiation collects in the body of anybody who works indoors all day.
Hospitals stand on ground whose rock gives out much more radiation.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that radiation dose may be affected by occupation; work with X-ray equipment and radioactive sources adds to her dose.

mcqs.q: People living where the local rock is granite, and aircrew who fly long-haul routes, both receive above-average annual radiation doses. Which statement explains both cases?
options: Fallout from nuclear weapons tests gathers on high ground and on granite.
Both groups spend much more of their working time above sea level.
Location affects dose: granite gives radon, altitude gives cosmic rays.
Dose depends only on occupation, so both groups must share a job.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the level of background radiation may be affected by location; radon from rock and cosmic rays are both natural sources whose level varies with where you are.

mcqs.q: A safety leaflet states that a worker received a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv during one year. What does this dose value describe?
options: The number of counts that her detector recorded each second.
The number of nuclei that decayed in the sources she used.
The mass of radioactive material she took into her body.
The risk of harm to her body from the radiation absorbed.
mcqs.explain: Radiation dose measures the risk of harm to body tissue from the radiation absorbed; it depends on the amount and the type of radiation.

mcqs.q: A patient's total radiation dose over a course of treatment is 2500 mSv. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?
options: 2.5 Sv
mcqs.explain: A millisievert is one thousandth of a sievert, so 2500 mSv is divided by 1000, giving 2.5 Sv.

mcqs.q: A worker's badge records a dose of 45 mSv over one year. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?
options: 45 Sv
4.5 Sv
mcqs.explain: 45 mSv divided by 1000 gives 0.045 Sv, correctly a smaller number than the value in millisieverts.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the half-life values of radioactive isotopes is correct?
options: They are all much the same, since every unstable nucleus decays at a similar rate.
They all lie between a few seconds and a few days, for any isotope at all.
They change with the temperature and the pressure a sample is kept at.
They cover a very wide range, from fractions of a second to billions of years.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.

mcqs.q: A radioactive isotope with a half-life of many thousands of years is spilled onto open ground. Why is such a long half-life a particular hazard here?
options: The ground stays radioactive for a very long time after the spill.
Its activity is enormous, so it emits a great deal of radiation now.
Isotopes with a long half-life always emit alpha, the worst kind of all.
It decays so fast that it spreads over the whole area at once.
mcqs.explain: A long half-life means the activity falls only very slowly, so the contamination remains a hazard for generations.

mcqs.q: A source with a half-life of a few minutes is spilled in a school laboratory. Why is it a serious hazard at once but much less of one an hour later?
options: The nuclei all stop decaying once one half-life has gone by.
Its activity is high at first and then falls away fast.
A short half-life means it gives out no radiation at all.
Its radiation changes from gamma into harmless alpha rays.
mcqs.explain: A short half-life means very many decays each second at the start, and that rate halves every few minutes, so the hazard is immediate but brief.

mcqs.q: A tracer is injected so that a doctor can watch how a patient's kidneys are working. Which property makes an isotope suitable for this use?
options: It emits alpha radiation, which is easily detected through the skin.
It has a half-life of many years, so the scan could be repeated later.
It emits radiation intense enough to destroy the tissue it reaches.
It emits gamma radiation, which leaves the body and is detected outside.
mcqs.explain: Gamma radiation is penetrating and weakly ionising, so it passes out to a detector while depositing comparatively little energy in the patient.

mcqs.q: How are nuclear radiations used to control or destroy a tumour lying deep inside the body?
options: A high dose of gamma radiation is aimed at the tumour from outside.
A weak alpha source is swallowed and travels to the tumour site itself.
A tracer is injected and its gamma rays then shrink the tumour.
The tumour is cooled by radiation until its cells stop dividing.
mcqs.explain: External beam radiotherapy uses a high dose of penetrating gamma radiation directed at the tumour, often rotated around the patient.

mcqs.q: A gamma-emitting tracer with a half-life of about six hours is chosen instead of one with a half-life of several years. Evaluate this choice.
options: Poor: a source that decays this quickly cannot give out enough radiation to be detected.
Good: the activity falls quickly, so the patient's dose after the scan stays small.
It makes no difference: the tracer leaves the body within a day whatever its half-life.
Poor: a longer-lived tracer would let the doctors scan the same organ again later.
mcqs.explain: A half-life of hours gives ample activity for imaging and then decays away, limiting the dose received once the scan is over.

mcqs.q: A scan using a radioactive tracer gives a patient a dose of about 6 mSv. The average annual dose from background radiation is about 2.7 mSv. The patient refuses the scan, saying that any nuclear radiation is too dangerous. Which is the best evaluation of that decision?
options: The dose is close to one year of background radiation, so there is no risk.
Refusing is right, because man-made radiation harms the body more than background.
The small added risk should be weighed against the benefit of a diagnosis.
Refusing is right, since a dose above background is certain to cause a cancer.
mcqs.explain: Evaluating a perceived risk against given data means comparing a dose of a few millisieverts with the consequences of leaving an illness undiagnosed.

mcqs.q: A gamma beam rotated around a patient destroys a deep tumour, but it also passes through healthy tissue. Evaluate this treatment.
options: Justified: the tumour is destroyed and the dose to healthy tissue is limited.
Ideal: careful aiming means that only the tumour receives any radiation.
Unjustified: no dose of nuclear radiation to a patient is acceptable.
Ineffective: gamma is too weakly ionising to damage a deep tumour.
mcqs.explain: Rotating the beam spreads the dose to healthy tissue over a large volume while the tumour stays in the path, so the benefit outweighs the side effects.
